name: Generalized Linear Model (GLM)
analogy: Think of it as one adjustable machine with a single weighted-sum engine and two interchangeable attachments. One attachment bends the engine's output into the right shape for your target, such as a probability or a count. The other says how much noise to expect at each level. Swap the attachments and the same machine handles direction, counts or sizes.

steps.title: Name the shape of the target
steps.description: The first decision is what kind of thing is being predicted: a yes-or-no outcome, a whole-number count, or an always-positive size. That choice decides which noise pattern the model assumes. A yes-or-no target, for example, is noisiest when the chance is near fifty-fifty.
steps.inExample: The target is whether the next 5-minute MNQ bar closes higher, a yes-or-no outcome, so the model assumes yes-or-no noise.

steps.title: Choose the bending curve
steps.description: A link curve connects the plain weighted sum to the quantity being predicted. It guarantees valid answers: probabilities stay between zero and one, counts and sizes stay above zero. For a yes-or-no target the standard choice is an S-shaped curve.
steps.inExample: The S-shaped curve is chosen, so any score, however large, maps to a chance between 0 and 100 percent.

steps.title: Build one weighted-sum score
steps.description: Every feature is multiplied by its weight and the results are added into a single score for the bar. All of the model's learning lives in these weights. Everything else, the curve and the noise pattern, is fixed by the choices above.
steps.inExample: The recent 15-minute fall and a momentum reading below 50 add to the score, near-average volume subtracts a little, and the total for the 10:30 bar comes out slightly positive.

steps.title: Fit the weights by repeated reweighted fitting
steps.description: The weights are found by solving a weighted line-fitting problem, then re-weighting every bar according to the new fit, and repeating until the weights stop changing. This reaches the exact most-likely weights for the chosen noise pattern, usually in a handful of rounds.
steps.inExample: On 20,000 past bars the fitting converges after 5 rounds.

steps.title: Judge the fit by deviance
steps.description: Fit quality is measured by deviance, a generalization of the sum of squared misses that suits any noise pattern. The model's deviance is compared with that of a no-feature model, which always predicts the average, to see how much the features actually explain.
steps.inExample: The fitted model's deviance on held-out later bars is only slightly below the no-feature model's, a small but real gain.

steps.title: Bend the score into the answer
steps.description: For a new bar the score is passed through the bending curve to give the expected value of the target, and each weight comes with a standard error telling how firmly it was pinned down.
steps.inExample: The slightly positive score passes through the S-shaped curve and becomes a 55 percent chance that the bar closes higher.

useFor.example: Estimating the chance that the next 5-minute MNQ bar closes higher from 35 base features, with an S-shaped bending curve.
Forecasting the number of trades or ticks in the next bar from volume and volatility, with a count-friendly curve.
Forecasting expected range or slippage in points, always above zero and with spread that grows with the size.
Comparing a model with and without the volume features and checking whether the improvement is bigger than chance before feeding them to a larger model.
Mapping a signal's strength to a recommended position size where each feature's contribution can be read off and explained.

avoidWhen: The relationship between features and target bends or depends on feature combinations; trees and neural networks find such structure while a GLM's single weighted sum cannot.
The target does not fit any of the standard noise patterns, such as a heavily multi-peaked distribution; a mixture model or a neural network that outputs a full distribution suits that better.

example.scenario: For a 10:30 five-minute MNQ bar, a GLM set up with yes-or-no noise and the S-shaped curve, trained on 20,000 past bars, is asked for the chance that the next bar closes higher.

input.summary: The family and curve choices, and one row of features for the bar that just closed.

fields.name: family and curve
fields.meaning: The choices that make the output a probability between 0 and 100 percent.

fields.name: move over the last 3 bars
fields.meaning: How far price has fallen over the previous 15 minutes.

fields.name: relative strength index, 14 bars
fields.meaning: A momentum reading from 0 to 100; below 50 means recent selling dominated.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading was compared with the recent norm.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar.

output.summary: The weighted-sum score and the probability it becomes.

fields.name: weighted-sum score
fields.meaning: The sum of each feature times its weight, before the bending curve; zero would mean even odds.

fields.name: probability the next bar closes higher
fields.meaning: The score after passing through the S-shaped curve.

fields.name: comparison with always guessing the average
fields.meaning: The share of up bars in the training data, the baseline a feature-free model gives.

example.reading: A 55 percent chance against a baseline near 50 percent is a faint lean. The same machine could be pointed at a count or a size just by changing the family and curve. Judge it on later bars by the deviance against the no-feature model and by whether trades at this lean cover costs.
